newsitem.title: UK: Britain sticks to "wait-and-see" on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Britain sticks to "wait-and-see" on EMU.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major's cabinet backed his "wait-and-see"approach to the European single currency on Thursday, but expressed strong doubts that some EU states would meet the criteria for entry in 1999.

Ministers agreed that if European Union states could not show their economies were capable of making the single currency sustainable in the long term, then it was better to delay rather than stick to the timetable, a senior government source said.

In a tough warning that Britain would not be dragooned into joining, the source said the cabinet agreed that if the single currency went ahead without the tough economic criteria being met, then "Britain would not be a part of it".

"We would only join if the conditions are right and it was in Britain's national interest," the source said after a cabinet meeting which reviewed a Treasury report on whether other European countries were "fudging" the single currency criteria.
The report was commissioned after Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke came under pressure in December from members of the cabinet opposed to closer European integration.

So-called "Eurosceptics" in the ruling Conservative party want Major to rule out entry into a single currency in the life of the next five-year parliament, believing this will be a vote winner in the election which is due by May 22 at the latest.
The opposition Labour party is well ahead in the polls.

But Clarke has fought a bitter defence of the current policy, which would allow Britain to decide whether or not to join the single currency when it goes ahead, even threatening to resign if Major bowed to the demands of the Eurosceptics.
Newspapers had billed Thursday's cabinet discussion as the last chance for Eurosceptics to get Major to change his mind.

But a change of policy became virtually impossible when Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind made it clear this week he believed neither the national nor the Conservative party's interests would be served by a hardening of the position.
There had been signs in recent weeks that Rifkind might move to a Eurosceptic position. Major has said a referendum will take place if the cabinet should ever decide to join the currency.

Clarke confirmed the cabinet had stuck to the "wait-and-see" policy, telling reporters: "We were proceeding on the basis of the policy that we're going to negotiate and decide at the right time, and that was accepted by everybody."
The opposition Labour party warned that growing anti-European sentiment in the Conservative party could scare foreign investors away from Britain.
Labour leader Tony Blair seized on a report in The Times newspaper that Japanese car giant Toyota was worried some Conservative "Eurosceptics" wanted to pull out of the EU.

Referring to the report, he said: "People know that Britain has to be part of Europe...Being a key leading player in Europe is in Britain's interests...for jobs, for investment and for our influence and standing in the world."

Labour is viewed as marginally more pro-European than the Conservatives although it has shifted towards a sceptical approach in recent months. Its attitude to a single currency is almost identical to the government's.
